doc.title: Ingrid Sertso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Woodstock, New York, August 11, 2014

title: Ornette Coleman and where free jazz goes next
summary: Monk Rowe opens in Woodstock and asks how music progresses from Ornette's free jazz; Ingrid calls Ornette the final word, and mentions the hippie joke.

story.theme_name: Opening the interview: Monk Rowe's welcome and archive boilerplate
story.community_name: Opening the Hamilton College interview: introductions and boilerplate

blocks.x: My name is Monk Rowe and I’m in Woodstock, New York. I’m very pleased to be in the home of Ingrid Sertso and Karl Berger. Thank you for letting me come. And I read an interesting thing in your Columbia interview, and I thought I would try it at the front door but I didn’t, and that was to ask, “Oh are there any hippies still here?” I can just picture someone, a complete stranger, “Where’s the hippies?” But anyway, it’s a pleasure to meet you and I’ve heard your name for many years, and Karl’s name. And I’d like to see if I could get a handle on some of the way you create music, and you know you’ve been in the forefront of this music for a long time. I was thinking about the fact that jazz is about a hundred years old, give or take, and it’s gone through so many styles and changes and back and forth, and getting more complex, simpler. And then I thought about the fact that Ornette Coleman did free jazz in the early sixties. How do you progress from that approach that Ornette Coleman did at that time? I don’t know if you use the word “free” in what you —
Okay. Well that music was pretty free to my ears. So if that was one of the first groundbreaking recordings, where does it go from there?

First of all, we have tourists coming up here that ask, roll your window down, “Is there any hippies around?” Just to answer what you asked before. Okay. Ornette invented the harmolodic approach to music and I think he helped us all to be confident in our need to really express ourselves freely. Where it goes from there, I wouldn’t know. For me, Ornette is the final, at the moment. Where it would go from there, I wouldn’t know. Because he is the most, that’s the most natural music to me. Ornette’s personal playing is very emotional, there’s a lot of feeling in it, and it goes away from the whole system of the bebop, you know, of all these changes jazz went through. And before we came here it was actually Ornette that brought us. Because I’m singing much longer than Karl. I grew up in an artist family. My brother is a well-known fantastic painter, all these pictures are from him; and my mother is a classical piano player. So for me music, that was it — not © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-
